entry.title: When should you to cash out in Vampire Crawlers
entry.summary:
Vampire Crawlers will force you to put on your thinking cap whenever you come across a treasure chest. You'll find these valuable treasures whenever you defeat a boss or by randomly exploring the map. Opening them will provide you with gems that you can equip on your cards. However, you can refuse them to get 200 Gold Coins to add to your inventory.
When exactly should you go for the latter and get rich?
Table of contents Vampire Crawlers cash out explained When to cash out in Vampire Crawlers
Vampire Crawlers cash out explained
Every treasure chest in Vampire Crawlers will have three gems on offer at random. You can pick one of them to add to an applicable card of your choice. There are some really powerful options you can avail that will radically change the strength of your deck.
Screenshot by Destructoid
However, you can opt to get 200 Gold Coins by choosing the 'cash out' option at the bottom. Doing so will immediately forfeit the gems on offer, and the treasure chest will disappear. If you're unsure, you can just 'leave' and return to the chest later before leaving the room.
When to cash out in Vampire Crawlers
I use two simple rules to decide when you should cash out a treasure chest.
Do you have a card to upgrade with a gem? Once you've applied a few upgrades, you won't have a card that's worth upgrading with a gem. It might also happen that the applied boosts will have negligible effects. If that happens, going for the Gold Coins will be beneficial.
Do you like the gems on offer? The offers are completely random, and it's highly possible that they won't be of any use to you. In such cases, it's always better to go for Gold Coins.
If you're unsure about how good/poor the gem offerings are, you can always check this guide to find out how they work.

How to heal and restore health in Vampire Crawlers
entry.summary:
Vampire Crawlers is a kind of game where taking damage (and reducing your HP in the process) is just a matter of one wrong decision. The deeper you go on your run, the higher the chances for your HP to take a hit.
Hence, you'll need to restore the lost health whenever possible for you to be considered successful.
How to heal in Vampire Crawlers
When you begin a run in Vampire Crawlers, you'll come across light sources. At first, the locations of these light sources will be hidden, and you'll need to depend on blind luck. Once you unlock the Guiding Light relic after reaching Inlaid Library, the locations of all light sources on the map will be shown.
Screenshot by Destructoid
When you break a light source, there will be a chance to find a floor chicken from it. When you consume this item, it will restore 10 HP. However, you should only consume it when your HP has reduced by 10 HP or more, since there's no overhealing.
Screenshot by Destructoid
You might also see mega stacks of floor chickens very rarely in food stalls, as shown in the image above. To activate the effect, you'll need to sacrifice a card from your deck. These mega stacks heal not 10, but 30 lost health. It's a game-changer if your HP is in a dire situation.
Finally, there's the Recovery Power Up that helps to restore your lost health. This Power Up restores one HP after an encounter. If you upgrade it three times (max), you'll get +3 HP after every battle. The number will feel less, but here's how you can use it efficiently.
Once you take a hit on your HP, don't go immediately into another boss battle. Instead, try the normal battles and avoid taking more hits. This will help you restore your HP and also allow you to gain Gold and XP. At this rate, you can restore 9-12 HP quite easily, and effectively make the most out of the Recovery Power Up.

Mezi aktuální témata patří podpora zařízení se Snapdragonem 845, například OnePlus 6/6T, Xiaomi Poco F1 nebo Shift 6MQ, a experimentování s FairPhone 5.
Účastníci si budou moci Linux přímo vyzkoušet na podporovaných telefonech a zapojit se do společného hackování. Akce je neformální a otevřená, dorazit je možné i jen na část dne.

entry.title: A little bit Black & White, a little bit Fable, Molyneux's citybuilder Masters Of Albion has the potential to break free of its influences – but it has a lot of work to do

If I don't beat down the undead creature soon, he'll break into the tomb and kill my character in his sleep, forcing me to restart the day. It should be easy to kill the monster, after all, I've two strapping heroes nearby, multiple ballista towers, and my godhand courses with lightning. But, for some reason my heroes have decided to attack other, less threatening monsters, my towers aren't shooting the ghoul, and my lightning bolts refuse to strike. Masters Of Albion, the new god game from Peter Molyneux's studio 22 Cans, fizzes with promise, but it has a lot of kinks to work out in early access if it's going to become more than a bucket of enjoyable mechanics. On paper, DLSS 5 is a chance for a simple PR win, a positive example of using AI to improve the performance of modern videogames. Instead, they offered an opportunity to make every game you own slightly uglier, and only if you can afford the dual-GPUs it requires to run. DLSS 5 is fascinating not just as an extension of Nvidia’s AI-first business philosophy, and not just as a sign of the slowdown in hardware advancement, and not just because of what it says about our desire for 'more real than real' graphics. DLSS 5 also reflects the world we find ourselves in today, perhaps the most neatly-packed microcosm I’ve seen to date. When I think of Idols of Ash, I think of seven sounds, listed here in order of deepening dreadfulness. The first and nicest sound is the clink of my silvery grapple sinking its hook, interrupting the rush of air past my ears as I fall. That's the second, less nice sound. The third sound is a distant, tectonic groaning, disconsolate and wakeful: it could be the wind again, pushing through some unaccountably musical lungful of stone. Yeah, I'm sure that's all it is.
The fourth sound is definitely not the wind: a squeaky, squidgy rumination, like the cooing of idle pigeons. You hear that cooing and you start running, because it generally precedes the fifth sound, the stiletto rattle of chitinous feet. When the legs are close, there's the sixth sound, a rasping, gaping hiss, and it's time to yeet yourself into the chasm while hurling your grapple towards the nearest jutting surface. With any luck, you will not then hear the seventh sound: the thud of your hook bouncing off the rock.

The final task: enduring the fearsome rattling and suspect braking of our dad’s neglected Renault Megane, just long enough for it to sputter to someone mad enough to buy it off us. The irony, that this clanking full-stop on the end our bereavement’s lengthy administrative aspect could so feasibly kill me, was not lost. That process, from the last beep of hospital machinery to the unhaggled exchange of French scrap metal, took 11 months, so it’s good that A Storied Life: Tabitha condenses its own house clearance to just a couple of hours. Posthumously asked by an elderly friend to give her cottage a tidy, you spend half your time in A Storied Life rummaging through her things in a kind of reverse Unpacking, selecting which bric-a-brac to throw away, which to keep, and which – with her blessings – to auction off for cash. The other half is spent taking inspiration from the objects you’ve kept to rewrite her water-damaged memoirs, a bittersweet series of word puzzles that still achieves a certain warmth – provided you can come to terms with the peculiar writing style.
